sections.title: Scope
lines: **Scope** decides which parts of the program can access a variable. JavaScript looks in the closest scope first, and then in the outer ones. This is called **lexical scope**: it depends on where the function is written.
```js
const tax = 0.19;            // General tax
function calculatePrice(price) {
const tax = 0.10;          // Local promotion
return price * (1 + tax);
console.log(calculatePrice(100)); // 110
console.log(tax);                 // 0.19

The local variable does not change the global one. `let` and `const` have **block scope** (`{}`); `var` has **function scope**. If a variable does not exist in any reachable scope, you get a `ReferenceError`.

**In an interview:** "Scope decides where a variable is visible. JavaScript uses lexical scope: a function can access the scope where it was defined and the outer scopes, but not the local variables of another function."

sections.title: Hoisting and the Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ)
lines: Before running a scope, JavaScript registers all its declarations. This is **hoisting**. It does not move lines of code: it only reserves the names before running the statements.
```js
const price = 100;
function calculate() {
console.log(price); // ReferenceError, it does not print 100
const price = 50;
calculate();

The local `price` takes priority in the whole function, but it is not initialized yet. That stretch is the **Temporal Dead Zone**. `var` starts as `undefined`; `let` and `const` cannot be read before their declaration. Function declarations like `function greet() {}` can be called before their line; `const greet = () => {}` cannot, because it follows the rules of `const`.

**In an interview:** "Hoisting means declarations are prepared before the code runs. If I read a `const` before it is initialized, I get a `ReferenceError`, even if an outer variable has the same name, because the local one is in the TDZ."

sections.title: Closures
lines: A **closure** happens when a function keeps access to the variables of the scope where it was created, even after the outer function has finished.
```js
function createCounter() {
let count = 0;
return () => ++count;
const usersCounter = createCounter();
const ordersCounter = createCounter();
usersCounter();  // 1
usersCounter();  // 2
ordersCounter(); // 1
Each call to `createCounter()` creates an independent scope. This is how you keep **private state** without exposing it.

**In an interview:** "A closure keeps access to the variables of the scope where the function was defined. I use it to hide state, to create configured functions, and for callbacks that need to remember data."

sections.title: this, arrow functions, call, apply and bind
lines: In regular functions, `this` depends on how the function is called: if you call a method through an object (`player.heal()`), `this` points to that object.
```js
const player = {
health: 50,
heal() {
this.health += 10;
player.heal(); // health = 60
const heal = player.heal;
heal(); // In strict mode: TypeError, this is undefined
When you separate the method from its object, the context is lost:
- **In strict mode** (always on in modules and classes): `this` is `undefined` and you get a `TypeError`.
- **Without strict mode** (scripts without `'use strict'`): `this` points to the global object (`window` in the browser). There is no error, but you change a global variable by accident.
Arrow functions do not have their own `this`: they use the one from the code around them. Here the arrow is inside `heal()`, so it uses its `this`, which is `player`:
```js
const player = {
health: 50,
heal() {
setTimeout(() => {
this.health += 10; // this is still player
That is why arrows do not work as methods of an object literal (an object created with `{}`): `heal: () => { this.health += 10 }` does not use `player`, but the outer `this`.
`call`, `apply` and `bind` let you set `this` explicitly:
```js
function heal(amount) { this.health += amount; }
const player = { health: 50 };
- `heal.call(player, 10)`: runs right away with `this` = `player`.
- `heal.apply(player, [10])`: same as `call`, but receives the arguments in an array.
- `heal.bind(player)`: returns a new function with `this` fixed, without running it.

**In an interview:** "In regular functions, `this` depends on how they are called; in arrow functions it is lexical. I use arrows to keep `this` in callbacks, and `bind` to fix it when I pass a method as a function."

sections.title: Callbacks
lines: A **callback** is a function you give to another function, so it can call it when it is the right time. It does not mean it is asynchronous.
```js
import { readFile } from 'node:fs';
readFile('config.json', 'utf8', (error, content) => {
if (error) return console.error(error);
console.log(content);
console.log('The read was already requested');

The last `console.log` does not wait for the file. The callback `(error, content)` follows Node's **error-first** convention. On the other hand, `products.filter(p => p.price < 10000)` calls its callback **synchronously**.
**In an interview:** "A callback is behavior passed as an argument. It can run right away, like in `filter`, or after an I/O operation, like in `readFile`."

sections.title: Promises, async and await
lines: A **Promise** represents a result that will arrive later. It can be `pending`, `fulfilled` or `rejected`. An `async` function **always returns a Promise**, and `await` **pauses that function only**, not the whole thread.
```js
async function loadDashboard(userId) {
const [profile, orders] = await Promise.all([
fetch(`/api/users/${userId}`).then(r => r.json()),
fetch(`/api/users/${userId}/orders`).then(r => r.json())
return { profile, orders };
Both requests start before waiting. **`fetch` does not reject on HTTP 404 or 500**: in production you check `response.ok`.
|Method|Result|
|`Promise.all`|All fulfill, or it rejects as soon as one rejects.|
|`Promise.allSettled`|Waits for all of them, including the rejected ones.|
|`Promise.race`|Takes the first result that finishes (fulfilled or rejected).|
|`Promise.any`|The first one that fulfills; rejects only if all of them reject.|

**In an interview:** "I use `async/await` for readability, and `Promise.all` when operations are independent. `race` is useful to compete against a timeout, but it does not cancel the other operations."

sections.title: Event Loop and Call Stack
lines: JavaScript runs on a single thread with a **Call Stack**: each called function is pushed onto the stack and leaves it when it finishes. The **Event Loop** moves pending tasks to the stack only when the stack is empty.
**Order of execution:**
1. **Synchronous code:** runs right away.
2. **`process.nextTick(fn)` (Node only):** schedules `fn` to run as soon as the synchronous code ends, before Promises. Node uses it internally; it is rare in your own code.
3. **Microtasks:** Promise callbacks (`.then()`, the code after an `await`). All of them run as soon as the stack is empty.
4. **Macrotasks:** `setTimeout` and I/O callbacks (network, files). After each one, the pending microtasks run again.
```js
console.log('A');                               // Synchronous
setTimeout(() => console.log('B'), 0);          // Macrotask
Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('C')); // Microtask
process.nextTick(() => console.log('D'));       // nextTick
console.log('E');                               // Synchronous
// Output: A, E, D, C, B
A `setTimeout` of `0` is not immediate: it is a minimum delay, and it waits for its turn.
**In practice:** heavy synchronous code (big loops, `JSON.parse` of a huge file) blocks the stack. In Node, the server stops responding in the meantime.

**In an interview:** "JavaScript runs on one thread. The Event Loop gives tasks to the Call Stack when it is empty: first `process.nextTick` and the microtasks, like Promises, and then timers and I/O. That is why in Node I avoid heavy synchronous work: it would block every request."

sections.title: Async patterns: order and concurrency
lines: **`forEach` vs. `for...of`.** `forEach` ignores what its callback returns, so it does not wait for its Promises. `for...of` (or any `for`/`while` loop) lets you wait for each operation before continuing.
```js
// ❌ Does not wait for the saves to finish
ids.forEach(async id => {
await save(id);
console.log('Done'); // Printed before they finish
// ✅ Waits for each save, in order
for (const id of ids) {
await save(id);
console.log('Done'); // All of them finished
**Unnecessary sequential `await`.** If two operations are independent, run them concurrently with `Promise.all`:
```js
// ❌ Sequential: 2 + 3 = 5 seconds
const a = await getA(); // 2 seconds
const b = await getB(); // 3 seconds
// ✅ Concurrent: about 3 seconds
const [a, b] = await Promise.all([getA(), getB()]);

**In an interview:** "I use `for...of` with `await` when operations must run in order, and `Promise.all` when they are independent. I avoid `forEach` with `async`, because it does not wait for the Promises."

sections.title: Limiting concurrency and handling errors
lines: `Promise.all` starts every operation at the same time. With thousands of them (for example, 10,000 emails), you can go over an API's limit (`429`, see [HTTP status codes](#node-status-codes)) or run out of database connections (see [connection pooling](#node-streams-pool-shutdown)).
**Option 1 — Batches:** process 50 at a time.
```js
for (let i = 0; i < ids.length; i += 50) {
const batch = ids.slice(i, i + 50);
await Promise.all(batch.map(id => sendEmail(id))); // Waits for the 50 before moving on
It is simple, but each batch waits for its slowest email: if one takes 10 seconds, the whole batch takes 10.
**Option 2 — `p-limit`:** an npm library that always keeps N operations running. As soon as one finishes, it starts another.
```js
const limit = pLimit(50); // import pLimit from 'p-limit'
await Promise.all(ids.map(id => limit(() => sendEmail(id)))); // Receives a function: p-limit decides when to start it

**Errors:** if one Promise fails, `Promise.all` rejects (you catch it with `try/catch`), but the others keep running. To get the result of all of them, including the failed ones, use `Promise.allSettled`.
**In an interview:** "With many operations, I limit concurrency with batches or `p-limit`. If I need to know which ones failed, I use `Promise.allSettled`."

sections.title: Immutability and references
lines: **Immutability** means not changing a shared value, but creating a new version of it. It matters in React because React **compares the references of the old and the new state** (`Object.is`). If you change the same object, React may not notice the change and skip the render.
```js
const [user, setUser] = useState({ name: 'Ana', age: 30 });
user.age = 31;                                   // Wrong: mutates the state
setUser(previous => ({ ...previous, age: 31 })); // Right: a new object
`{ ...previous }` is a **shallow copy**: nested objects still share references, so you must copy them too:
```js
setUser(prev => ({ ...prev, address: { ...prev.address, city: 'Santiago' } }));

`structuredClone(obj)` creates a **deep copy**: it duplicates everything nested. It is useful to get an independent copy, but it does not support functions. It is not a good fit for React state, because it creates new references even for the parts that did not change, so memoized components render again for no reason.

**In an interview:** "Immutability avoids changing shared data and makes changes easy to detect. In React it matters because React compares references to notice state updates. With nested objects, I also have to create new references for them."

sections.title: Pure functions and side effects
lines: A **pure function** returns the same result for the same arguments, and it does not change anything outside itself. A **side effect** can be writing a file, changing an outside variable or making a request.
```js
let discount = 0.10;
const impure = price => price * (1 - discount); // Depends on something outside
const pure = (price, discount) => price * (1 - discount);
**In an interview:** "A pure function depends only on its arguments and has no visible effects. I test it with inputs and outputs, without faking a database, the network or global state."

sections.title: Coercion, == and ===
lines: **Type coercion** is converting values between types. `==` allows implicit conversions; `===` compares without converting.
```js
const requestedId = '15';         // req.params.id arrives as a string
15 == requestedId;                // true (coercion)
15 === requestedId;               // false
15 === Number(requestedId);       // true (explicit conversion)
**In an interview:** "I prefer `===` and explicit conversions, and I validate inputs like HTTP parameters to avoid `NaN` or unexpected results."

sections.title: Prototypes and prototypal inheritance
lines: In JavaScript, a **prototype** is an object that other objects can inherit properties and methods from, without copying them. This is called **prototypal inheritance**.
When you read a property, JavaScript first looks for it in the object. If it is not there, it looks in its prototype, and then in that prototype's prototype. This is the **prototype chain**.
**Example:**
```js
const numbers = [1, 2];
numbers.push(3); // [1, 2, 3]
Why can we call `push()` if we never defined it? Because arrays inherit that method from `Array.prototype`.

**In an interview:** "JavaScript uses prototypal inheritance to share methods and properties between objects. When a property does not exist in an object, JavaScript looks for it in its prototype chain. Modern classes use this mechanism internally."

sections.title: ES Modules vs. CommonJS
lines: A **module** is a file that exports code so other files can import it. Node has two module systems:
```js
// CommonJS (CJS): Node's original system
const fs = require('fs');
module.exports = { parse };
// ES Modules (ESM): the JavaScript standard, also in the browser
import fs from 'node:fs';
export function parse() {}
**Key differences:**
- **When they load:** `require` loads the file when that line runs. `import` is resolved before the file runs, so an invalid import fails before any code runs.
- **How Node chooses:** it uses ESM if the file ends in `.mjs` or if `package.json` has `"type": "module"`. Otherwise it uses CommonJS.

- **Mixing them:** an ESM file can import a CommonJS one. The other way around, `require` of an ESM file used to fail; Node 22+ allows it, unless that file uses `await` outside a function (**top-level await**).

**In an interview:** "I prefer ES Modules because they are the standard, shared by Node and the browser. CommonJS is still in many projects and libraries, so I can read it and I know how Node decides which one to use."

sections.title: Debounce and throttle
lines: Two techniques to limit how many times a function runs when an event happens very often (typing, scrolling, resizing the window):
- **Debounce:** waits until the event stops for some time, and only then runs. Example: search when the user has not typed for 300 ms, instead of sending a request on every key.
- **Throttle:** runs at most once per interval, even if the event keeps happening. Example: update the scroll position every 100 ms.
```js
function debounce(fn, delay) {
let timer;                                      // The closure remembers the timer between calls
return (...args) => {
clearTimeout(timer);                          // Cancels the pending run
timer = setTimeout(() => fn(...args), delay); // Schedules a new one
const search = debounce(query => fetchResults(query), 300); // fetchResults: calls the API
input.addEventListener('input', e => search(e.target.value));
Each key cancels the previous timer, so only the last search runs. The timer lives in a [closure](#js-closures). Real projects usually use a library version, like the one in `lodash`.

**In an interview:** "I use debounce when only the last event matters, like a search while typing, and throttle when I need regular runs, like while scrolling. Both avoid unnecessary work and requests."

sections.title: Quick reminders
lines: - **`'use strict'`:** turns on stricter rules to avoid common mistakes. For example, it does not let you assign undeclared variables. ES modules and classes turn it on automatically.
```js
'use strict';
age = 30; // ReferenceError: age is not declared
- **`null` vs `undefined`:** `undefined` means no value was assigned; `null` means "no value" on purpose.
- **`const`:** stops you from reassigning the variable, but it **does not freeze** the object.
- **`map` / `filter` / `reduce`:** transform / select / accumulate. Do not overuse `reduce` if a loop is easier to read.
- **Spread/rest (`...`):** spreads values or creates shallow copies; as a parameter, it groups the arguments.
- **`??` and `?.`:** `count ?? 10` uses `10` only if `count` is `null` or `undefined` (`||` would also replace a `0`). `user?.address` returns `undefined` instead of throwing an error.

sections.title: What does TypeScript add?
lines: **TypeScript** adds **type checking before the code runs**. It finds contract errors between modules, but **types disappear when compiling**: on their own, they do not validate a JSON that arrives over the network.
```ts
function sendReceipt(email: string): void { /* ... */ }
sendReceipt(123); // TypeScript error before running
If `123` comes from an external API, the compiler cannot see it: you need **runtime validation** (see [Zod](#ts-zod)).
**In an interview:** "TypeScript adds static typing, makes refactoring easier and documents contracts. It does not replace tests or the validation of external data."

sections.title: type, interface and optional properties
lines: `interface` usually describes object contracts; `type` can also describe unions, tuples and combinations.
```ts
interface User { id: number; name: string; nickname?: string }
interface Admin extends User { permissions: string[] } // Extends with interface
type AdminAlt = User & { permissions: string[] };       // Same idea with type
type UserId = string | number;                          // Union: only with type

`?` marks an **optional property**: it may not exist in the object. One practical difference: if you declare the same `interface` twice, TypeScript merges them (**declaration merging**); with `type`, you get an error.
**In an interview:** "I use `interface` for object contracts and `type` for unions and combinations. What matters most is being consistent."

sections.title: Union types, narrowing and exhaustive switch
lines: A **union** lets a value have several types or shapes.
- **Discriminant:** a property that identifies each variant, like `type`. A union with this property is a **discriminated union**.
- **Narrowing:** TypeScript reduces the possible types when you check a condition (`if`, `switch`, etc.).
- **`never`:** a type with no possible values. It lets you check that you handled every variant.
```ts
type PaymentEvent =
| { type: 'paid'; amount: number }
| { type: 'refunded'; reason: string };
function describe(event: PaymentEvent): string {
switch (event.type) {
case 'paid':
// Narrowing: event is the 'paid' variant
return `Paid: ${event.amount}`;
case 'refunded':
// Narrowing: event is the 'refunded' variant
return `Refund: ${event.reason}`;
default: {
// No variants left: event is never
const unreachable: never = event;
return unreachable;
**What is `never` for?** If we add a `'pending'` variant without its `case`, TypeScript shows an error on `const unreachable: never = event`. This way we find forgotten cases at compile time.
**In an interview:** "Unions represent variants of data. With narrowing, TypeScript identifies each variant through conditions, and with `never` I check that a `switch` handles every possible case."

sections.title: Generics
lines: **Generics** let you write reusable functions **without losing the concrete type**.
```ts
function first<T>(items: T[]): T | undefined {
return items[0];
const id = first([10, 20]); // number | undefined
With `any`, you would lose that information. We return `undefined` because the list could be empty.
**In an interview:** "A generic reuses logic and keeps the type guarantees: if it receives `User[]`, it returns `User`, not `any`."

sections.title: any, unknown, assertions and type guards
lines: `any` turns off type checking. `unknown` forces you to **check** the type before using it. `as User` (a **type assertion**) does not convert or validate anything: it only tells the compiler to trust you.
A **type guard** is a function that does the check and teaches the result to the compiler:
```ts
function isUser(value: unknown): value is User {
return typeof value === 'object' && value !== null
&& 'id' in value && 'name' in value;
const payload: unknown = await response.json();
if (isUser(payload)) {
payload.name; // Here TypeScript knows it is a User
**In an interview:** "I treat external input as `unknown` until I validate it. Assertions help the compiler, but they do not protect you from wrong data at runtime."

sections.title: Runtime validation with Zod
lines: Writing type guards by hand for big objects is tedious. With **Zod** you define a **schema** that **validates at runtime**, and **the type comes from it**, so you do not keep two definitions:
```ts
import { z } from 'zod';
const CreateIssueSchema = z.object({
title: z.string().min(1).max(100),
assigneeId: z.string().optional()
type CreateIssueDTO = z.infer<typeof CreateIssueSchema>;
const result = CreateIssueSchema.safeParse(req.body);
if (!result.success) {
return res.status(400).json({ errors: result.error.issues });
// result.data is a CreateIssueDTO, already validated
`safeParse()` returns a result that you check with `if`; `parse()` throws an exception if the data is not valid.
That is why a [DTO](#arch-dto-mapping) defined only as a type is not enough: it validates nothing at runtime; the schema does. In NestJS the usual tool is `class-validator`, with the same idea.
**In an interview:** "I keep one source of truth: the schema validates the request at runtime, and the TypeScript type is inferred from it."

sections.title: Utility types and other reminders
lines: **Utility types** create new types from other types, so you do not repeat definitions.
```ts
type User = { id: string; email: string; age: number };
type Update = Partial<User>;               // All properties optional
type Contact = Pick<User, 'id' | 'email'>; // Selects properties
type WithoutAge = Omit<User, 'age'>;       // Removes properties
type Scores = Record<string, number>;      // String keys, number values
type UserKeys = keyof User;                // 'id' | 'email' | 'age'
const guest = { name: 'Ana', age: 30 };
type Guest = typeof guest;                 // { name: string; age: number } (type of a value)
type Email = User['email'];                // string (type of that property)

**`as const`:** TypeScript usually infers wide types: `'admin'` becomes `string`, because you could change it. `as const` says the values will not change, so the type keeps the exact value and marks it `readonly`.
```ts
const a = { role: 'admin' };          // { role: string }
const b = { role: 'admin' } as const; // { readonly role: 'admin' }
A typical use: write a list of values once, and get a union type from it:
```ts
const ROLES = ['admin', 'member'] as const;
type Role = typeof ROLES[number]; // 'admin' | 'member'
// typeof ROLES: the type of the array
// [number]: the type of the element at any index (number is a type, not a variable)
// Without as const, Role would be string
**Other concepts:**
- **`readonly`:** stops properties from being reassigned in TypeScript, not at runtime.
- **`strict: true`:** a `tsconfig.json` option that turns on strict checks to find more errors.

**In an interview:** "I use utility types to reuse definitions. `Partial` makes properties optional, `Pick` selects, `Omit` removes and `Record` defines keys and values. These types only exist at compile time: `Omit`, for example, does not remove real properties from an object."

sections.title: What is Node.js?
lines: **Node.js** runs JavaScript outside the browser, using V8 (Chrome's JavaScript engine) and server APIs. It is great for systems with a lot of **I/O** (network, files, databases).
"Single-threaded" is a simplification: your JS code runs on one thread, but Node hands off the heavy work:
- **Network:** handled by the operating system.
- **Files, cryptography:** processed by a group of internal Node threads (the **thread pool**), without blocking your code.
- **Your own heavy calculations:** you move them to [Worker Threads](#node-worker-threads), extra threads you create to run JavaScript in parallel.

**In an interview:** "Node is ideal for apps with a lot of concurrent I/O, like APIs. Its weak spot is heavy calculations on the main thread: they block the event loop and the server stops responding."

sections.title: API layers and responsibilities
lines: In an API, it is common to split the code into **layers**, where each one has a specific job. This makes the code easier to maintain, test and reuse.
- **Route:** defines the URL and the HTTP method (`POST /tasks`) and sends the request to the controller.
- **Middleware:** runs logic before the controller, like authentication, body validation or logging.
- **Controller:** receives the request, calls the service and builds the HTTP response.
- **Service:** holds the business rules, like not allowing tasks in closed projects.
- **Repository:** wraps data access, like PostgreSQL queries.
- **DTO (Data Transfer Object):** defines the shape of the data sent or received, so you do not expose unnecessary information.
**Example flow:**
1. The client sends `POST /tasks` with a title and a token.
2. Middlewares authenticate and validate the body.
3. The controller calls `createTask(userId, title)`.
4. The service applies permissions and business rules.
5. The repository saves to PostgreSQL.
6. The controller responds `201` with a DTO.
This way you can test the rule "no tasks in closed projects" without starting an HTTP server. The full path, with the domain and the mapper, is in [How it all connects](#arch-flow).

**In an interview:** "I separate responsibilities: middlewares authenticate and validate, the controller handles HTTP, the service applies the business rules and the repository handles persistence. This way I can test and change each layer on its own."

sections.title: REST and HTTP methods
lines: **REST** is an API style where URLs represent resources (`/tasks/1`) and the HTTP method says what to do with them.
The HTTP standard describes methods with two properties, used in the table:
- **Safe:** it only reads; it does not create, change or delete data. It has nothing to do with security. Example: `GET`.
- **Idempotent:** repeating the same request leaves the data the same as running it once. Example: `DELETE`.
|Method|Usual use|Relevant property|
|`GET /tasks`|Read|Safe and idempotent|
|`POST /tasks`|Create|Usually not idempotent|
|`PUT /tasks/1`|Replace|Idempotent if well designed|
|`PATCH /tasks/1`|Change part of it|May or may not be idempotent|
|`DELETE /tasks/1`|Delete|Idempotent in its effect|
**Example:**
- `DELETE /tasks/1`: the first request deletes the task; the next ones change nothing else. The response can change (`204` and then `404`), but the data does not.
- `POST /tasks`: sending a request to create a task three times could create three different tasks.
Idempotency matters most when a request fails because of the network and the client needs to **retry without creating duplicate changes**.

**In an interview:** "Idempotency means that repeating a request has the same effect as running it once. For example, deleting a resource several times does not change the final result. It is important for safe retries after network failures."

sections.title: HTTP status codes
lines: The **status code** tells the result of a request. The first digit tells the family: **2xx** success, **4xx** client error, **5xx** server error.
**2xx — Success**
- `200` OK: success with content.
- `201` Created: a resource was created.
- `204` No Content: success without content (for example, a `DELETE`).
**4xx — Client error**
- `400` Bad Request: a badly formed request (for example, invalid JSON or a missing field).
- `401` Unauthorized: valid authentication is missing. Despite the name, it is about authentication.
- `403` Forbidden: authenticated, but without permission.
- `404` Not Found: it does not exist, or it is hidden for security reasons (see [BOLA / IDOR](#sec-bola)).
- `409` Conflict: it clashes with the current data (for example, the email is already registered).
- `422` Unprocessable Content: the format is correct, but the data breaks a rule (for example, the end date is before the start date). Some APIs use `400` for both cases.
- `429` Too Many Requests: the [rate limit](#node-resilience) was exceeded.
**5xx — Server error**
- `500` Internal Server Error: an unexpected error.
- `503` Service Unavailable: the service is down or temporarily overloaded.
**In an interview:** "I use consistent status codes, I tell 401 apart from 403, and I never expose internal details in a 500."

sections.title: Middleware, validation and error handling
lines: A **middleware** is a function that runs in the chain of a request, in the order it was registered (authentication, validation, logging). It receives `(req, res, next)` and does one of two things: it responds and stops the chain, or it calls `next()` to go to the next one.
- **`next()`:** goes to the next one, but the code after `next()` still runs. That is why people often write `return next()`.
- **`next(error)`:** skips the normal middlewares and goes straight to the **error handler**.
**Two ways to create a middleware:**
**1. Direct:** when it only needs `(req, res, next)`. You register it by passing the function as it is (`authenticate`).
```js
function authenticate(req, res, next) {
if (!req.headers.authorization) {
return res.status(401).json({ message: 'Not authenticated' }); // Stops the chain
next(); // Goes to the next one

**2. Factory (middleware factory):** when it also needs a value you choose when registering the route, like the schema to validate. Express only gives it `(req, res, next)`, so that value is passed to an outer function that returns the middleware. You register it by calling it (`validateBody(userSchema)`).
```js
function validateBody(schema) {
return (req, res, next) => {
const result = schema.safeParse(req.body); // Zod
if (!result.success) {
return res.status(400).json({ errors: result.error.issues });
next();
It is a [closure](#js-closures): the returned middleware remembers `schema`. `validateBody(userSchema)` runs once, when the route is registered; the middleware it returns runs on every request.
**Example with Express:**
```js
const userSchema = z.object({ name: z.string(), age: z.number() });
app.post('/users',
authenticate,              // Direct
validateBody(userSchema),  // Factory
async (req, res, next) => {
try {
const user = await userService.create(req.body);
res.status(201).json({ id: user.id });
} catch (error) {
next(error); // Sends the error to the handler
app.use(errorHandler); // Error handling

**`errorHandler(err, req, res, next)`:** Express recognizes it by its 4 parameters (with 3, it treats it as a normal middleware) and only calls it when there is an error. That is where each error is translated to its HTTP status code (see [domain errors](#arch-domain-errors)).

**Sync or async?** Either one, because it is just a function. If a middleware awaits a query that takes 2 s, the next one waits: Express only moves on when `next()` is called or a response is sent. If neither happens, the request hangs.
**Errors in `async` functions:**
- **Express 4:** does not catch the **rejected promise**, so the error never reaches the `errorHandler`. That is why the route in the example uses `try/catch` + `next(error)`.
- **Express 5:** calls `next(error)` automatically, so that `try/catch` is not needed.

**In an interview:** "I use middlewares for authentication and validation, services for business rules and one central error handler to respond to errors consistently. They can be sync or async: the chain moves on with `next()`, and in Express 4 async errors are passed with `next(error)`."

sections.title: Timeout, retry, rate limiting and idempotency
lines: These mechanisms help you handle failures and protect your APIs:
- **Timeout:** sets a maximum waiting time, so you do not wait forever.

- **Retry:** tries again after temporary failures (network, `503`, `429`), with a limit of attempts. It is only safe for [idempotent](#node-rest-methods) operations; otherwise, you use an idempotency key.
- **Exponential backoff:** increases the wait between retries (1 s, 2 s, 4 s) so you do not overload a service that has problems.
- **Rate limiting:** limits the requests per client (for example, 100 per minute); above that, it responds `429`.
**Idempotency example:**
A client sends `POST /payments` with an **idempotency key** and loses the response. When it retries with the same key, the server recognizes the payment and does not charge again.
- **Client:** creates a unique key per operation (the `Idempotency-Key` header) and reuses it on retries.
- **Server:** stores the key with the result. A **unique constraint** prevents processing it twice, even with simultaneous requests.

**In an interview:** "I use timeouts to limit waits, retries with exponential backoff for temporary failures and rate limiting to control traffic. For payments, I use idempotency keys so a retry does not charge twice."

sections.title: Webhooks
lines: A **webhook** is an HTTP request that **another system sends to your API** when something happens. Instead of your backend asking every minute "is it paid yet?" (**polling**), the provider tells you.
**Example:** you register the URL `https://api.myshop.com/webhooks/stripe` in Stripe. When a payment is completed, Stripe sends a `POST` to that URL with the payment data.
To receive them correctly:

- **Verify the signature:** anyone could send a `POST` to your URL. That is why the provider signs each webhook with a secret key it shares with you, and sends the signature in a header (for example, `Stripe-Signature`). Your API calculates the signature again and rejects the webhook if it does not match, just like with a [JWT](#sec-jwt).
- **Respond fast:** if your API is slow or fails, the provider retries. That is why you respond `200` right away and leave the heavy work in a [queue](#arch-eda).
- **Idempotency:** because of those retries, the same webhook can arrive twice. You store the event ID and ignore repeated ones (see [idempotency](#node-resilience)).

**In an interview:** "A webhook is an HTTP notification that an external system sends to my API when an event happens. I verify its signature, respond fast and process it idempotently, because the provider can retry it."

sections.title: CORS and cookies
lines: **CORS** (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) is a browser policy that controls which sites can read an API's responses from JavaScript.
- **Origin:** protocol + domain + port. `https://app.com` and `https://api.app.com` are different origins.
- **How it works:** the API responds with the header `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://app.com`. If the page's origin is not allowed, the browser blocks the response.

- **Preflight:** if the request can change data or is less common (for example, `PUT`, `DELETE` or a JSON body), the browser first asks for permission with an `OPTIONS` request: "can app.com send you a DELETE?". Only if the API accepts does it send the real request. A simple `GET` is sent directly.
**It is not authentication:** `curl` (a terminal command for HTTP requests) or another server can call the API anyway, because they do not apply CORS.

**Cookies between origins:** cookies travel in the `Cookie` header (for example, `Cookie: sessionId=abc123`), which the browser adds automatically. This is how the API knows which user is making the request.
But if your page (`app.com`) calls an API on another origin (`api.app.com`), the browser does not add the cookies by default, with any HTTP method. To send them, both sides must agree:
- **Frontend:** asks to include them with `fetch(url, { credentials: 'include' })`.

- **API:** responds `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true` and names the exact origin. With cookies, `*` (any origin) is not allowed, because any site could use the user's session and read the response.
The security attributes of cookies (`HttpOnly`, `Secure`, `SameSite`) are in [Where to store tokens](#sec-token-storage).

**In an interview:** "The browser applies CORS to control which origins can read my API's responses; it does not replace authentication. If I use cookies between origins, I turn on credentials and allow explicit origins."

sections.title: Events and EventEmitter
lines: An **event** is a notice that something happened. With **EventEmitter** (from `node:events`, included in Node), an object emits events and other parts of the code react by registering callbacks (**listeners**).
```js
import { EventEmitter } from 'node:events';
const orders = new EventEmitter();
orders.on('created', order => console.log('Email to', order.email)); // 1. Registers the listener
orders.emit('created', { email: 'ana@mail.com' });                   // 2. Emits: runs the listener
- **`on`:** the listener runs every time the event happens (`once`: only the first time).
- **`emit`:** it is synchronous: it runs every listener before moving to the next line.
- **`'error'`:** if it is emitted and nobody listens to it, the process crashes.
- **Event vs. Promise:** a Promise settles once; an event can happen many times.

Node uses it in servers, streams and workers (for example, `worker.on('message')`, see [Worker Threads](#node-worker-threads)). It works inside one process; events between services are something else (see [event-driven architecture](#arch-eda)).

**In an interview:** "EventEmitter lets an object announce that something happened, and other parts react with listeners, without knowing each other. Unlike a Promise, an event can happen many times."

sections.title: Streams, connection pooling and graceful shutdown
lines: These mechanisms improve the performance and stability of a Node.js app.
**Streams:** process files or data in chunks, without loading them fully into memory. They are useful to send big files:
```js
app.get('/export', (req, res) => {
createReadStream('export.csv').pipe(res); // From node:fs
`pipe()` sends the file to the client (`res`) in chunks. If the client receives slowly, it pauses the reading so memory does not fill up (**backpressure**).

**Connection pooling:** opening a database connection is slow (network, authentication). A **pool** keeps connections open and gives a free one to each query; if all of them are busy, the query waits. The database library manages it (Prisma and TypeORM have their own):
```js
const pool = new Pool({ max: 10 });      // pg library, once at startup
await pool.query('SELECT * FROM users'); // The pool picks the connection

**Graceful shutdown:** during a deploy, the platform (Docker, Kubernetes) sends `SIGTERM`, an operating system **signal** that asks the process to stop. By default, Node cuts the requests in progress; you set up the orderly shutdown yourself:
```js
const server = app.listen(3000);
process.on('SIGTERM', () => {
server.close(() => pool.end()); // Rejects new ones, waits for current ones and closes the DB
**In an interview:** "I use streams for big files, a pool to reuse database connections, and graceful shutdown with SIGTERM so requests are not cut during a deploy."

sections.title: Worker Threads
lines: A **Worker Thread** is an extra thread inside the same Node process, for heavy calculations: this way the main thread keeps serving requests (see [What is Node.js?](#node-what)).
- **Entry file:** the worker runs a file, which can import functions from anywhere in the project. You cannot pass it a function directly.
- **Messages:** they do not share variables; they send copied values (objects, strings), like with `structuredClone` (see [immutability](#js-immutability)).
- **When to use them:** only for CPU work (parsing, compressing, processing images). With I/O (database, network) they do not help, because Node already handles it without blocking.
```js
// main.js (main thread)
import { Worker } from 'node:worker_threads'; // Included in Node
const worker = new Worker('./csv-worker.js', { workerData: users }); // 1. Creates the thread with data
worker.on('message', csv => console.log(csv)); // 4. Event: runs when the message arrives
```js
// csv-worker.js (worker)
import { workerData, parentPort } from 'node:worker_threads';
import { jsonToCsv } from './parser.js';
const csv = jsonToCsv(workerData); // 2. Heavy calculation
parentPort.postMessage(csv);       // 3. Sends the result (triggers 'message')
**In an interview:** "I use Worker Threads only for heavy CPU calculations, so I do not block the event loop. For I/O they are not needed, because Node already handles it without blocking."

sections.title: Memory leaks
lines: A **memory leak** happens when the app keeps data it no longer uses, but that is still referenced. Because of that, the **garbage collector** (the JavaScript mechanism that frees memory nobody uses) cannot delete it. Memory grows with each request, until the server gets slow or crashes.
**Typical causes:**
- **Cache without a limit:** a global object that stores results and never deletes anything.
- **Listeners that are never removed:** each request adds an `.on(...)` (see [EventEmitter](#node-events)) and `.off(...)` is never called.
- **Timers that are never cleared:** a `setInterval` that keeps running and referencing data.
```js
const cache = {}; // Lives as long as the process lives
app.get('/users/:id', async (req, res) => {
cache[req.params.id] = await getUser(req.params.id); // getUser queries the DB; cache grows with each ID and is never emptied
res.json(cache[req.params.id]);

**How to avoid and find them:** limit the size of caches (or use Redis with expiration) and remove listeners and timers you no longer need. The warning sign is memory usage that only goes up in the [metrics](#arch-observability). To find the cause, you take a **heap snapshot** (a picture of the memory) with Chrome DevTools.

**In an interview:** "A memory leak is memory that is still referenced even though it is no longer used. In Node it usually comes from caches without a limit, or from listeners and timers that are never cleaned up. I find it with memory metrics and heap snapshots."

sections.title: HTTP cache and versioning
lines: The **HTTP cache** reuses responses to avoid repeated queries. The server sets it up with headers and the browser applies it on its own.
- **`Cache-Control`:** how long and where to store the response.
- `public, max-age=60`: 60 seconds, even in caches shared between users (**shared cache**), like a CDN (servers spread around the world that deliver copies from the closest one, like Cloudflare).
- `private`: only in the user's browser. For personal data.
- `no-store`: it is not stored.

- **`ETag`:** a hash of the response's version. When the cache expires, the browser sends it back (the `If-None-Match` header); if nothing changed, the server responds `304 Not Modified` with no body.
```js
app.get('/products', (req, res) => {
res.set('Cache-Control', 'public, max-age=60'); // The catalog is the same for everyone
res.json(products); // Express generates the ETag on its own
**API versioning:** `/v1/` and `/v2/` let you change the contract without breaking old clients.
**In an interview:** "I use `Cache-Control` and `ETag` to reuse responses, `private` for personal data, and I version the API when there are incompatible changes."

sections.title: Authentication vs. authorization
lines: **Authentication:** proving who you are. **Authorization:** checking what you can do with a specific resource.

**Example:** Ana logs in correctly (authentication), but tries `DELETE /projects/42`. Even if her token is valid, she must not be able to delete the project if she is not an admin (authorization). We respond `403`.
**In an interview:** "I authenticate the identity and authorize every action on every resource. A valid JWT does not mean the user can access any record."

sections.title: BOLA / IDOR: the most common API flaw
lines: **BOLA** (Broken Object Level Authorization), also called **IDOR** (Insecure Direct Object Reference), happens when the API checks that you are authenticated, but not that the resource **belongs to you**. It is risk #1 in the **OWASP API Security Top 10**, the list of API risks published by OWASP, a well-known web security organization.
```ts
// Vulnerable: by changing the ID in the URL, any logged-in user can read other users' invoices
const invoice = await repo.findById(req.params.id);
// Correct: the query requires the invoice to belong to the user
const invoice = await repo.findOne({ id: req.params.id, ownerId: req.user.id });
if (!invoice) return res.status(404).end();
Responding `404` instead of `403` avoids confirming that the resource exists.
**In an interview:** "On every endpoint that receives an ID, I check that the resource belongs to the user or that they have permission on it. Validating the token is not enough."

sections.title: RBAC and per-resource permissions
lines: Two ways to decide what an authenticated user can do:
- **RBAC** (Role-Based Access Control): permissions depend on the role (`admin`, `member`, `viewer`).
- **ABAC** (Attribute-Based Access Control): permissions depend on attributes of the user or the resource, like "is the owner" or "is a member of the project".
In practice they are combined: "a `member` can edit issues, but only in the projects they belong to".
```ts
const canEdit = user.role === 'member'                  // RBAC: the role allows editing
&& project.memberIds.includes(user.id);               // ABAC: belongs to the project

**In an interview:** "I use roles for general permissions and I check membership of the resource on every operation. Authorization lives in the backend; hiding buttons in the frontend is not security."

sections.title: What is a JWT?
lines: A **JWT** (JSON Web Token) is a signed token that identifies the user. It is commonly used for **authentication**.
**How it works:**
1. The user logs in and the server gives them a signed JWT.
2. The client sends it on every request: `Authorization: Bearer <token>`.
3. The server checks the signature and the expiration, without querying a sessions database. This makes it easier to scale with several servers.
**What is inside?** A JWT is a text with three parts separated by dots: `header.payload.signature`.
- **Header:** says the token type and the algorithm used to sign it (for example, `HS256`).
- **Payload:** holds the user's data, called **claims**. For example, `sub` (the user's ID) and `exp` (when the token expires). The server reads them to know who is making the request.

- **Signature:** the server creates it when it creates the token, by combining the header, the payload and a secret key that only it knows. When it receives the token, it calculates the signature again: if someone changed the payload (for example, changed `sub` to another user's ID), the signature no longer matches and the token is rejected.
**Watch out:**
- The payload is only encoded in Base64, which anyone can decode without a key. Do not put sensitive data in it.
- You cannot invalidate it before `exp` unless the server stores a list of revoked tokens. That is why access tokens are short-lived (see [refresh tokens](#sec-login-sessions)).

**In an interview:** "A JWT is a signed token that the server verifies without querying the database, which makes scaling easier. Its payload is readable, so I do not store secrets there, and I use short expirations because it is hard to revoke."

sections.title: Login flow, sessions and refresh tokens
lines: **Login flow:**
1. The user sends their email and password over HTTPS, and the server compares the password with its [hash](#sec-passwords-secrets).
2. If it is correct, it gives an access token or creates a server-side session (see below).
3. On every request, the server checks who the user is and whether they have permission on the resource (see [BOLA](#sec-bola)).
**Access token vs. refresh token:**
- **Access token:** sent on every request. It is short-lived (for example, 15 minutes): if it is stolen, it is useful only for a short time.
- **Refresh token:** lasts longer (for example, 7 days) and is only used to ask for a new access token when the current one expires.
Since the refresh token lasts longer, it is protected with:
- **Rotation:** each use gives a new one and invalidates the previous one. If someone reuses an old one, the server detects the theft.
- **Revocation:** the server stores the valid ones so it can invalidate them, for example on logout.

**Server-side session:** the alternative to tokens. The server stores the session (in the database or Redis) and the client only gets its ID in a cookie. It is easy to revoke by deleting it, but it is looked up on every request.
**In an interview:** "I use short-lived access tokens and refresh tokens with rotation. If I need to revoke sessions easily, I use server-side sessions."

sections.title: OAuth2 and OpenID Connect
lines: - **OAuth2:** lets an app access the user's resources in another service without knowing their password. Example: your app reads the user's Google Calendar with an **access token** that Google gives it.
- **OpenID Connect (OIDC):** a layer on top of OAuth2 that also says **who the user is**, with an **ID token**: a [JWT](#sec-jwt) with their ID and email. It is what is behind "Sign in with Google".
**Authorization Code flow** (the recommended one):
1. Your app redirects the user to Google, which asks them to log in and accept the permissions.
2. Google sends them back to your app with a **temporary code** in the URL.
3. Your app exchanges that code for the tokens, directly with Google.

**PKCE** (Proof Key for Code Exchange): protects step 3. At the start, your app creates a random secret and sends Google only its hash. When it exchanges the code, it sends the original secret. This way, if someone steals the code, they cannot exchange it without the secret.
**In an interview:** "OAuth2 delegates permissions and OIDC adds identity. For external login I use Authorization Code with PKCE, which stops a stolen code from being used."

sections.title: Where to store tokens: XSS and CSRF
lines: When deciding where to store the token in the browser, you must think about two attacks:
- **XSS** (Cross-Site Scripting): an attacker manages to run malicious JavaScript in our page and can read data or act as the user.
- **CSRF** (Cross-Site Request Forgery): a malicious site makes the browser send a request to our API, and the browser attaches the cookies of the active session on its own.
**Where to store it?**

- **`localStorage`:** the frontend sends the token by hand in the `Authorization` header. Since the browser does not attach it on its own, there is no CSRF risk; but JavaScript can read it, so an XSS attack could steal it.

- **`HttpOnly` cookie:** JavaScript cannot read it, so an XSS attack cannot steal it (although it could still make requests from our page). But the browser attaches it automatically, so you must protect yourself from CSRF.
**Protections for cookies:**
- **`Secure`:** the cookie is only sent over HTTPS.
- **`SameSite`:** the browser does not send it in requests started from other sites.
- **CSRF token:** a random value that the server gives to our page and requires on every request that changes data. A malicious site cannot know it.

**In an interview:** "I prefer `HttpOnly` and `Secure` cookies, because an XSS attack cannot steal them, and I protect against CSRF with `SameSite` or CSRF tokens. With `localStorage` there is no CSRF, but the token is exposed to XSS."

sections.title: Passwords and secrets
lines: **Passwords:** they are stored as a **hash**, a transformation that cannot be reversed. At login, the server hashes the password the user typed and compares it with the stored hash.
- **Slow on purpose:** if someone steals the database, they can try millions of passwords (**brute force**). A slow algorithm is not noticeable in one login, but it makes that attack very expensive.

- **Recommended:** `Argon2id` (preferred), `scrypt` or `bcrypt`. They combine the password with a **salt**, a random value that is different for each user, so the same passwords produce different hashes.
- **Do not use `SHA-256`:** it is too fast.
- **Limit login attempts** with [rate limiting](#node-resilience), to slow down brute force against the API.

**Secrets** (API keys, database credentials): they are not hashed, because the app needs to use them. They go in a **secrets manager** (like Azure Key Vault or AWS Secrets Manager), which encrypts them and controls who can access them, or in the server's environment variables. Never in the repository, the logs or the frontend. If one leaks, you rotate it: you replace it with a new one and invalidate the old one.
**In an interview:** "I store passwords with slow algorithms like Argon2id, I limit login attempts and I keep secrets in a secrets manager, never in the code or the logs."

sections.title: Injection and least privilege
lines: **SQL injection** happens when user data is mixed into the text of a query and ends up running as SQL.

The main defense is **parameterized queries**: the query and the data travel separately, and the database treats the data only as a value, never as code. ORMs (Prisma, TypeORM) do it automatically, except when you write raw SQL by joining text (for example, `$queryRawUnsafe` in Prisma).
```js
const input = "' OR '1'='1";
// Vulnerable: the quote in the input closes the email text
db.query(`SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = '${input}'`);
// WHERE email = '' OR '1'='1'  → always true, returns every user
// Safe: $1 is a placeholder that is only replaced as a value
db.query('SELECT id, name FROM users WHERE email = $1', [input]);
// Looks for an email equal to the text "' OR '1'='1"  → finds nobody
**Principle of least privilege:** every user, process and account has only the permissions it needs. For example, the database user that the app uses can read and write data, but not drop tables.
**In an interview:** "I use parameterized queries, validate inputs, authorize per resource and apply least privilege. All external data is untrusted."

sections.title: Separation of Concerns
lines: **Separation of Concerns:** splitting the code so each part handles only one kind of task, like receiving HTTP, applying business rules or accessing the database. This way, each change touches only the part it belongs to.

**Example:** if tomorrow only admins can close tasks, that change goes in the task service, not in three endpoints or in the repository. This way, the same rule applies whether the order comes from the API, from a worker (a background process that consumes a queue, see [event-driven architecture](#arch-eda)) or from a terminal script.
**In an interview:** "I separate HTTP transport, business rules and persistence, so I do not repeat decisions and I can test them on their own. I do not add layers that do not make things clearer."

sections.title: Controller / route handler
lines: The **controller** is the HTTP entry point: it reads the parameters and the body of the request, calls the business logic and turns the result into a response. In Express it is the function registered for a route (**route handler**).
```ts
async function createIssueHandler(req, res) {
// issueService: class with the business rules for tasks
const issue = await issueService.create(req.user.id, req.body);
// toIssueResponse: function that picks which task fields are returned to the client
res.status(201).json(toIssueResponse(issue));
It does not contain business rules: if tomorrow the same action runs from a worker or a script, the rule must not be trapped in the controller.
**In an interview:** "I prefer thin controllers: they translate HTTP and delegate the important rules."

sections.title: DTO and data mapping
lines: A **DTO** (Data Transfer Object) is the contract of the data that goes into or out of an operation. **Mapping** is the function that turns the object that comes from the database or the domain into that contract: the DTO defines the shape and the mapper fills it. This way, a storage detail does not become a public contract.
```ts
// DTO
type IssueResponseDTO = { id: string; title: string; status: string };
// Mapping function
function toIssueResponse(issue: Issue): IssueResponseDTO {
return { id: issue.id, title: issue.title, status: issue.status };
The mapper builds the response only with the allowed fields, so you never return a `password_hash` or an internal field by accident.
An `Omit<User, 'password_hash'>` is not enough: it only changes the type, but the real object still has the field, and `res.json(user)` would send it anyway.

**In an interview:** "I use DTOs to make clear what each operation accepts and returns, and a simple mapper so I do not leak the persistence model. A DTO as a type does not validate anything: a schema does the validation."

sections.title: Format validation vs. business rules
lines: Both are validations, but they differ in what you need to decide:
- **Format:** looking at the received data is enough. Example: "`title` is a string of 1 to 100 characters". It is validated at the entry point, with a schema (Zod), before reaching the logic.

- **Business rules:** you need context, like who the user is or the state in the database. Example: "only project members can create tasks" or "an archived project cannot be changed". They are validated in the service or use case, which has that context.

**In an interview:** "I separate format validation from business rules. I validate the format at the entry point with a schema, because TypeScript does not check HTTP data at runtime; I validate business rules in the service."

sections.title: Service layer and use case
lines: Business logic can be organized in two ways:
- **Service** (service layer): a class that groups the operations of one area. Example: `IssueService` with `create()`, `close()` and `assign()`.
- **Use case:** one class for each business action, with a single method. Example: `CreateIssue` with `execute()`.
Both receive their dependencies from outside (see [Dependency Injection](#arch-di-dip)) and know nothing about HTTP.
```ts
class CreateIssue {
constructor(
private repo: IssueRepository,          // Data access
private permissions: PermissionChecker, // Checks if the user can create
async execute(userId: string, input: CreateIssueDTO) {
if (!(await this.permissions.canCreate(userId, input.projectId))) {
throw new ForbiddenError();           // Business error
return this.repo.create(input);

**In an interview:** "I organize business logic in services or use cases, separated from HTTP and persistence. I move to use cases when a service grows too much: each action gets its own class, easy to test."

sections.title: Domain model and invariants
lines: The **domain** is the code that represents the business concepts (projects, tasks) and their rules, without depending on HTTP or the ORM. An **invariant** is a business rule that must never break, wherever the change comes from.
```ts
// Domain: only applies the rule, no database or HTTP
function closeIssue(issue: Issue): Issue {
if (issue.status === 'archived') throw new IssueArchivedError();
return { ...issue, status: 'closed' };
// Service: loads, uses the domain and saves
async function closeIssueService(issueId: string, repo: IssueRepository) {
const issue = await repo.findById(issueId);
return repo.save(closeIssue(issue));

The service coordinates the steps; the domain decides whether the change is valid. This way, the rule applies the same way if the call comes from REST or from a worker. With concurrency, two simultaneous requests could pass the check at the same time, so some invariants also need [transactions or database constraints](#db-locking).
**In an interview:** "The domain holds the behavior and the restrictions of the business. I keep those rules out of HTTP and the ORM, so they apply from any entry point."

sections.title: Repository pattern
lines: A **data access interface**: the service asks for `findById` or `save` without knowing the SQL.
```ts
interface IssueRepository {
findById(id: string): Promise<Issue | null>;
save(issue: Issue): Promise<void>;
**Watch out:** it does not guarantee that you can switch PostgreSQL for MongoDB without changing anything, and you do not need to wrap every ORM method.
**In an interview:** "I use repositories when they improve isolation and testing. In a simple CRUD, an extra layer on top of the ORM can be redundant."

sections.title: How it all connects
lines: A request goes through the layers in this order, and each one has a single responsibility:
HTTP request
→ Middleware: authenticates and validates the format
→ Controller: builds the input DTO and calls the service
→ Service: checks permissions and coordinates the steps
→ Repository: loads the data from the database
→ Domain: applies the invariants (no database or HTTP)
→ Repository: saves the result
→ Mapper: turns the entity into the response DTO
HTTP response

A worker (a background process that consumes a queue, see [event-driven architecture](#arch-eda)) goes straight to the service, without passing through the controller. That is why business rules do not go in the controller.

**In an interview:** "The middleware validates the format, the controller adapts HTTP, the service coordinates, the domain applies the rules and the repository persists. This way, each change touches a single layer."

sections.title: Dependency Injection (DI) and Dependency Inversion (DIP)
lines: - **DI is a technique:** a class receives its dependencies from outside instead of creating them.

- **DIP is a principle:** high-level code (the *what*: business rules, like `IssueService`) depends on a contract (an interface that defines which operations exist, like `IssueRepository`), not on low-level code (the *how*: technical details, like `PostgresIssueRepository`). This way you can change the implementation without touching the service.
```ts
class IssueService {
constructor(private repo: IssueRepository) {} // Depends on the contract (DIP)
const service = new IssueService(postgresRepo); // Production (DI)
const testService = new IssueService(fakeRepo); // Test
In TypeScript, interfaces are erased at runtime, which is why NestJS uses tokens or classes to inject dependencies.

**In an interview:** "DI helps me follow DIP, but they are different things: the principle is about the direction of dependencies; injection is about how they are delivered. You can do DI by hand, without a framework."

sections.title: Domain errors and error mapping
lines: - **Domain error:** a custom error class that describes a business failure, like "the project is archived". It knows nothing about HTTP.
- **Error mapping:** a function, in one single place, that translates each domain error to an HTTP status code. It is called from the [error handler](#node-middleware).
```ts
class ProjectArchivedError extends Error {}  // Domain error
function mapDomainError(error: Error): number {
if (error instanceof ProjectArchivedError) return 409;
if (error instanceof ForbiddenError) return 403;
return 500; // Unknown error: respond without internal details
This way, the domain throws `ProjectArchivedError` without knowing what a 409 is. If the same rule runs from a worker, which does not use HTTP, the error still makes sense.
In NestJS this is done with an exception filter.
**In an interview:** "I use explicit business errors and one central mapper to HTTP. I never put `res.status()` inside the domain."

sections.title: Observability: logs, metrics and traces
lines: **Observability** is being able to understand what happens inside a system in production, from the data it emits. It is based on three kinds of data:
- **Structured log:** the record of an event in JSON format, easy to search and filter. Example: `{ "level": "info", "path": "/orders", "requestId": "abc123" }`.
- **Metric:** a number measured over time, like requests per second or response time.
- **Trace:** the path of a request, with how long each step took (Node, database, another service).
The `requestId` is a unique ID assigned to each request and included in its logs and traces, so you can find them together.
**Example — an endpoint takes 2 seconds:**

- The **metric** shows that the p95 went up from 200 ms to 2 s. The p95 (95th percentile) means that 95% of requests take that long or less, and the slowest 5% take more. Unlike the average, it does not hide that slow group.
- The **trace** shows that 1.8 s were spent in PostgreSQL, not in Node.
- With the `requestId`, the **logs** of that request show which user and which parameters caused it.
Together, they tell you where to look: check the indexes and the SQL plan before refactoring the controller.

**In an interview:** "I combine structured logs, metrics and traces linked by `requestId`. I measure before optimizing, and I never log passwords or tokens." A good follow-up is a real case where metrics or traces helped you find a slow part of a system.

sections.title: Monolith vs. microservices
lines: These are **system** architectures: they decide how many applications the system is split into and how they are **deployed** (published to production).
- **Monolith:** a single application with everything (users, orders, payments), deployed as a whole. It is simple to develop, test and debug.
- **Microservices:** each area is a separate application, with its own database, and they talk over the network (HTTP or [events](#arch-eda)). Each team deploys and scales its part on its own.

**The cost of microservices:** what is a function call in a monolith becomes a request over the network, which can be slow or fail. You also need more infrastructure and [observability](#arch-observability).

**When to use them:** when several teams block each other (for example, publishing a change in payments forces you to coordinate with the users team), or when one part needs to scale very differently from the rest. For a small team or a new product, a monolith is usually better.

**In an interview:** "I would start with a modular monolith and split out a service only for a concrete reason, like scale or team independence. Microservices solve organizational problems, but they add operational complexity."

sections.title: Modular monolith
lines: A **modular monolith** is a single deploy (see [monolith vs. microservices](#arch-monolith-microservices)), split inside into modules by business area. Each module exposes a **public interface**: the functions other modules can use. The rest is internal.
src/
orders/
payments/
index.ts    → exports only chargeOrder() (public interface)
stripe.ts   → internal: nobody outside payments imports it
users/
- `orders` charges with `import { chargeOrder } from '../payments'`. It never imports `stripe.ts` or reads the `payments` tables.
- If `payments` needs to scale on its own, it is extracted as a microservice: only what is behind `chargeOrder()` changes (for example, an HTTP request), and `orders` does not notice.
- In NestJS, each `Module` groups an area and exports only what is needed.
**In an interview:** "The modular monolith is my starting point: a single deploy, with clear limits between modules that make it easier to extract a service later if needed."

sections.title: Clean Architecture
lines: Clean, Hexagonal and DDD are **application** architectures: they organize the code *inside* an application. They are combined with system architectures (see [monolith vs. microservices](#arch-monolith-microservices)); for example, a monolith with Clean Architecture.
**Clean Architecture** organizes code in rings, like the layers of an onion. Its **dependency rule**: code in one layer can only import code from more inner layers.
Frameworks and drivers → Express, the PostgreSQL library                (outside)
Adapters             → controllers, the class that saves tasks in PostgreSQL
Use cases          → CreateIssue: create a task
Domain           → Issue and its rules, like closeIssue           (inside)
- The domain imports nothing from Express or the ORM: if you change frameworks, the rules are not touched.
- You can test use cases and the domain without a database or HTTP.
- **Watch out:** in a simple CRUD (an app that only saves and reads data, without complex rules), so many layers can be too much.

**In an interview:** "In Clean Architecture, dependencies point inward: the domain and the use cases do not know the framework or the database. This way I test the logic without infrastructure and change technical details without touching the rules."

sections.title: Hexagonal Architecture
lines: **Hexagonal** (or **ports and adapters**) organizes the code so the business logic does not depend on external technologies. It splits the application into two zones:
- **Core:** the business logic, that is, the [domain](#arch-domain) and the [services or use cases](#arch-service-usecase).
- **Outside:** the technical parts: Express, PostgreSQL, an email service.
The core never imports anything from the outside. They connect like this:
- **Port:** an interface that the core defines to say which operations it needs, without saying how they are done.
- **Adapter:** a class from the outside that implements that interface with a specific technology.
It is the same structure as [Dependency Inversion](#arch-di-dip):
```ts
interface IssueRepository { save(issue: Issue): Promise<void> }         // Port (core)
class PostgresIssueRepository implements IssueRepository {/* PostgreSQL SQL */} // Adapter (outside)
class IssueService {                            // Service (core)
constructor(private repo: IssueRepository) {} // Receives the port, does not know Postgres exists
const service = new IssueService(new PostgresIssueRepository()); // At app startup
In tests, you pass it another adapter: `new IssueService(new FakeIssueRepository())`, which stores in memory instead of the database.
A port can have several adapters. Example: `PaymentGateway` with `StripePaymentGateway` and `PayPalPaymentGateway`; the service charges the same way and only the adapter it receives changes.
**Two kinds of adapters:**
- **Output (driven):** the core uses them to talk to the outside. Example: `PostgresIssueRepository`.
- **Input (driving):** the outside uses them to call the core. Example: an HTTP controller that receives the request and calls the service.
**Relation with [Clean Architecture](#arch-clean):** they are variants of the same idea, protecting the business logic from technical details. In interviews they are often treated almost as synonyms.
Do not confuse it with the [Adapter pattern](#oop-structural): it is the same idea, at the scale of one class.

**In an interview:** "In Hexagonal, the core defines interfaces (ports) with what it needs, and the outside implements them (adapters), like a PostgreSQL repository. This way I can change the technology or use fake adapters in tests without touching the business logic."

sections.title: Domain-Driven Design (DDD)
lines: **DDD** is a way to design software starting from the business: the business concepts, words and rules are reflected directly in the code. It is not a folder structure. Key concepts:
- **Ubiquitous language:** the code uses the same words as the business. Example: `issue.close()`, not `updateStatus(3)`.
- **Bounded context:** each area of the business has its own model, because the same word means different things in each one. Instead of one giant `Customer` class with everything:
```ts
// Sales: cares about the customer's contacts
type Customer = { id: string; contacts: Contact[] };
// Billing: cares about their tax ID and address
type Customer = { id: string; taxId: string; address: string };

- **Aggregate:** a group of objects that share rules. Example: an order (`Order`) and its items: you cannot add an item to an order that was already shipped. The group is only changed through its **aggregate root**, which checks those rules (see [invariants](#arch-domain)):
```ts
order.addItem(item);    // ✓ Order checks that it was not shipped before adding
order.items.push(item); // ✗ adds straight to the list and skips the rule
Bounded contexts are good candidates for [modules](#arch-modular-monolith) or [microservices](#arch-monolith-microservices).
**Watch out:** it pays off in complex domains; in a simple CRUD it is too much.

**In an interview:** "DDD is modeling from the business: I use its language, I separate bounded contexts with their own models and I protect the invariants in aggregates. I apply it when the domain is complex."

sections.title: Event-driven architecture (EDA)
lines: In an **event-driven architecture** (**EDA**), services do not call each other directly: they publish **events** ("order created") to a **broker**, an intermediate service that delivers them to whoever listens (RabbitMQ, Kafka, Azure Service Bus). Unlike [EventEmitter](#node-events), these events travel between services over the network.
**Two ways of delivering:**
- **Queue:** each message is processed by only one consumer. It is used to split work.
- **Pub/sub:** each subscriber gets a copy. Example: orders publishes "order created", and emails and billing react separately.
**Why use it:** if billing goes down or there is a spike of orders, the events wait in the broker and are processed later. Meanwhile, orders keeps working.
**The cost:**
- **Eventual consistency:** the other services find out with a delay. Example: the email arrives a few seconds after the order.

- **Idempotency:** a message can arrive twice, so processing it again must not duplicate effects (see [idempotency](#node-resilience)). Messages that fail again and again are moved to a separate queue (**dead-letter queue**) to be reviewed.

**In an interview:** "In EDA, services talk through events using a broker. This way they are decoupled and absorb load spikes, at the cost of eventual consistency and idempotent consumers. In a past project, I used queues to move slow work out of the request."

sections.title: Comparing architectures
lines: The architectures in this chapter answer different questions, so they are combined instead of competing:
|Architecture|Question it answers|Good when…|
|[Monolith](#arch-monolith-microservices)|How many apps do I deploy? → one|Small team or new product|
|[Microservices](#arch-monolith-microservices)|How many apps do I deploy? → several|Teams that block each other, or parts that scale very differently|
|[Modular monolith](#arch-modular-monolith)|How do I split business areas inside one app?|Almost always, as a starting point|
|[EDA](#arch-eda)|How do the parts communicate?|Async processes or load spikes|
|[Clean](#arch-clean) / [Hexagonal](#arch-hexagonal)|How do I separate business logic from technology?|The logic must be tested without a database or HTTP|
|[DDD](#arch-ddd)|How do I model the business in code?|Complex domain, with many rules|
|[Vertical Slice](#arch-vertical-slice)|Do I group code by layer or by feature?|Many independent operations, with little shared logic|

**Example of a combination:** a modular monolith with the modules `orders` and `payments`, split by their bounded contexts (DDD). Each module organizes its code with Hexagonal. If `payments` is later extracted as a microservice, it talks to `orders` through events (EDA).

**In an interview:** "I do not choose a single architecture: I combine a system one, like a modular monolith, with an application one, like Hexagonal, and I add DDD or events only if the problem justifies it."

sections.title: Vertical Slice Architecture
lines: **Vertical Slice** organizes code by **feature**, not by technical layer. Each **slice** contains everything one operation needs: endpoint, validation, logic and data access.
By layers                      By slices
controllers/                   features/
orders.controller.ts           create-order/
services/                          create-order.handler.ts  → endpoint + logic
orders.service.ts                create-order.schema.ts   → validation
repositories/                    cancel-order/
orders.repository.ts             cancel-order.handler.ts
- **Advantage:** a change in "create order" touches one folder, and each slice can be as simple or as complex as it needs (one uses the ORM directly; another, domain rules).
- **Cost:** logic can be duplicated between slices. Shared logic, like the rules of an order, goes in a common module.
- **Combination:** each module of a [modular monolith](#arch-modular-monolith) can be organized in slices. Unlike [Clean](#arch-clean) or Hexagonal, it does not force layers inside each slice.

**In an interview:** "With layers, I group code by technical type; with vertical slices, by feature, so each change stays in one place. I prefer it when there are many independent operations and little shared logic."

sections.title: API Gateway and Saga
lines: Two common patterns in microservices:

**API Gateway:** a single entry point for all clients. It receives each request and sends it to the right microservice (`/orders` → orders, `/payments` → payments). It also centralizes what every service needs, like authentication, rate limiting and logs (**cross-cutting concerns**). This way, the client does not need to know each service. Examples: Kong or AWS API Gateway.

**Saga:** a transaction guarantees "all or nothing", but only inside one database, and each microservice has its own (see [microservices](#arch-monolith-microservices)). A saga replaces that guarantee: it is a sequence of steps, each one in its own service, and if one fails, **compensating actions** run to undo the previous ones.
Create order → Charge → Reserve stock ✗
Compensate: refund → cancel order
It can be coordinated in two ways:
- **Orchestration:** a central service tells each one what to do.
- **Choreography:** each service reacts to the events of the previous one (see [event-driven architecture](#arch-eda)).

**In an interview:** "The API Gateway centralizes the entry point and what all services share, like authentication. For operations across services I use sagas with compensations, because no transaction can span several databases."

sections.title: Circuit Breaker
lines: It protects your service when another service it depends on is failing. Instead of calling it again and waiting for timeouts, **it stops calling it for a while** and fails fast.
It works like an electrical switch: closed lets current pass, open cuts it. It has three states:
- **Closed:** normal; calls go through and failures are counted.
- **Open:** after several failures in a row, it stops calling and responds right away with an error or an alternative (**fallback**).
- **Half-open:** after some time, it lets a few test calls through. If they work, it goes back to closed; if they fail, it goes back to open.
**Example:** the payments service goes down. After 5 failures, the circuit opens for 30 s and the app shows "payments not available" instead of waiting.
